metadata.title: Time and Waves
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: Pulses, loops and ripples from one clock

beats.narration_text: Time and Waves. Learn what a shader's clock really counts, and how one sine wave with four numbers makes a pulse, a loop or a ripple.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Every shader can read a clock, called time. Most people expect it to start when their node appears. It does not. It starts when the game starts, and every shader reads the same one.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. Fragment is the function that runs once for each pixel. A uniform is a value your game sets from outside. U V is a point's address on the shape. A texture is an image a shader can read. And sine is a function that swings smoothly between minus one and one.

beats.narration_text: A shader cannot count: every frame it starts fresh, remembering nothing from the last. So the engine hands it a clock called time, the seconds since the engine started. One clock, shared by the whole game.

shot.visual_intent: The real Godot 4.7 canvas item shader page in a browser window, scrolled to the Global built-ins table. The camera pushes in on the TIME row and a terracotta ring marks 'Global time since the engine has started, in seconds.' The first line of the row is also the glossary wording on screen: 'TIME · seconds on one clock shared by the whole game'.

beats.narration_text: Two things you might expect to matter. The game's time scale does: at one half, the clock runs at half speed for every shader. Pausing does not. Scripts freeze, but the shimmer carries on.

shot.visual_intent: A real render: a grey track with a teal marker that a script moves by delta (top), and below it a square pulsing on TIME. At about 25 percent of the beat the time scale drops to one half: the marker and the pulse both slow. At about 60 percent the tree is paused: the marker freezes and the pulse carries on. Labels 'time scale 0.5' then 'paused'. Caption: 'time scale: how fast the game's clock runs · 1 is normal'.

beats.narration_text: The clock also has a limit. It wraps back to zero after thirty-six hundred seconds, one hour, by default. A pulse that repeats a whole number of times in that hour will not notice. Any other pulse jumps once.

shot.visual_intent: A horizontal clock bar labelled 'default limit: 3,600 s · one hour' with a terracotta marker that runs to the right end and wraps back to 0. Beneath it a zoom, labelled 'shown with the limit at 2 s so it fits on screen' (the measured check): time from 0 to 4 s, the wrap marked at 2 s and at 4 s. Two curves on it: the upper one (speed 1, two whole cycles in 2 s) carries on unbroken through each wrap; the lower one (speed 0.7, 1.4 cycles) snaps to a different height at each wrap, a vertical gap ringed in terracotta. Labels: 'a whole number of cycles: no jump' and 'any other: one jump'. Small grey credit: 'Apple M4 Pro · Godot 4.7.2 · limit set to 2 s · pulse change at the wrap: 4 steps against 44 (of 255)'.

beats.narration_text: To time a node from its birth, you might reach for the engine's tick counter, and subtract. Do not. It starts earlier than time: about a quarter of a second on this Mac, and a little different every run.

shot.visual_intent: Two horizontal rulers in seconds, one above the other. The top, labelled 'tick counter' (with the real call name in grey, Time.get_ticks_msec()), starts at 0 on the left. The bottom, labelled 'TIME', has its 0 a little to the right. Terracotta markers run along both at the same pace. A bracket between the two zeros reads 'about 0.25 s on this Mac'. A small cross over a subtraction sign between the two ruler labels lands on the words 'Do not'. Small grey credit: 'Apple M4 Pro · Godot 4.7.2 · three runs: 0.26, 0.29, 0.26 s'.

beats.narration_text: To start counting when a node appears, count it yourself. Add delta, the seconds since the last frame, to an age, and pass the age to the shader as a uniform. Now the late square starts its pulse from the beginning.

shot.visual_intent: GDScript card at left (the age counter, five lines). At right a real render: the left square pulses on TIME; a second square is added late and starts its pulse from the beginning, out of step with the first. Labels 'TIME' under the left square and 'age' under the right. Caption: 'delta: seconds since the last frame'.

show.event: the age += delta line highlighted
the set_shader_parameter line highlighted
the late square appears and starts from the beginning of its pulse

props.code:
var age := 0.0

func _process(delta):
	age += delta
	material.set_shader_parameter("age", age)

beats.narration_text: So choose by the job. A loop that never needs to start: use time. An effect that begins with a node: use an age. A one-time effect: use a uniform your game moves when the moment comes.

beats.narration_text: Now the wave. Put the clock inside a sine, and the value swings smoothly between minus one and one. Sine counts in angles, so one full swing takes six point two eight seconds. That number is tau.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'The Wave' (serif 40) top-left. Axes: time in seconds along x (0 to 13), value from -1 to 1 up the side. A terracotta dot travels along y = sin(TIME) at the pace of the clock, tracing the curve. A bracket under the first full swing reads 'one swing = 6.28 s'. At the end a label 'TAU = 6.28 · one full turn' lands beside the bracket (glossary: the number of radians in a full turn).

beats.narration_text: A color cannot go below zero, and sine does, half the time. Send a raw sine to a color and every negative value is clamped to zero. The pulse sits at its darkest for half of each swing.

beats.narration_text: So squeeze it into zero to one. Halve the swing, then lift it by a half. Zero point five plus zero point five times sine never leaves the range, and it still swings once per second.

beats.narration_text: Four numbers describe a sine wave. The first is amplitude: how far it swings from its middle. Shrink it and the pulse gets shallow; at zero it stops. A half is the most that fits in zero to one.

A bracket from the middle to a crest is labelled 'amplitude'. Caption: 'amplitude: how far the wave swings from its middle'. A grey note: 'a half is the most that fits in 0 to 1'.

beats.narration_text: The second is speed: how quickly it repeats. Time times speed counts the cycles, one cycle being one full swing. Speed one half gives a swing every two seconds. Speed two gives two swings every second.

beats.narration_text: The third is offset: where in its cycle the wave starts. Offset a quarter starts it at the top. Offset a half swings exactly opposite to a wave with none: when one is brightest, the other is darkest.

The two markers travel the strips in opposite directions. Caption: 'offset: added to slide the wave', second line 'here: where in its cycle it starts'.

beats.narration_text: Here are all three as uniforms, dials your game can set. Time times speed, plus offset, counts the cycles. Offset is an instance uniform, so each node can keep its own. The fourth number waits for a shape.

Cue labels: 'hint_range: the editor limits it to 0 to 0.5' on the amplitude line, 'instance uniform: each node keeps its own value' on the offset line and 'a fourth dial waits here: frequency' on the empty line.

beats.narration_text: Sine always swings back. For a loop that starts over, like a loading bar, use fract. It keeps only the part after the decimal point, so the cycle count becomes a ramp from zero to one, restarting every cycle.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Loops and Curves' (serif 40) top-left. A rising straight line (the cycle count TIME × speed, which never stops) with whole-number ticks 0, 1, 2, 3 up the side. A copy of the line is cut at every whole number and drops back to 0, becoming a sawtooth between 0 and 1. A ramp strip with a marker under it jumps back to the left at every restart. Labels (glossary wording): 'fract(x): the part after the point: x minus floor(x)' and 'ramp: a smooth run of values from 0 up to 1'.

beats.narration_text: To go back and forth at a steady pace, fold the ramp: double it, subtract one, take the absolute value, and subtract that from one. You get a triangle, rising and falling at the same rate.

shot.visual_intent: The sawtooth from the previous picture transforms in four small steps, each labelled: '× 2' (it now runs 0 to 2), '− 1' (−1 to 1), 'abs' (a V shape), '1 −' (flipped into a triangle). The strip marker now moves back and forth at a steady pace. Caption: 'abs(x): drops the minus sign'.

beats.narration_text: Same pace, three personalities. The sine eases into each turn. The triangle turns sharply. The sawtooth never turns back: it climbs, then jumps to the start. Pick the one whose motion you want.

Labels at the left of the rows: 'sine', 'triangle', 'sawtooth'. Caption: 'sawtooth: a ramp that restarts'.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Time is one clock for the whole game; count your own with an age. Time times speed counts cycles, and a sine turns the count into a pulse. Fract, a fold or a curve turns the same count into another loop. Feed the count from the address, and the wave travels across a shape. Four numbers set any sine wave: amplitude, frequency, speed and offset. Time keeps the beat; a uniform picks the moment.
